meta.tagline: The quiet giant of order, neon and perfection

pills: Most Michelin stars of any city
Tradition and future side by side

overview.title: Welcome to Tokyo
overview.intro: Tokyo is not one city but a hundred nested ones: five minutes separate the human tide of Shibuya Crossing from the cedar forest of Meiji Shrine. Here the world's densest metro doesn't slip by a second, the smallest ramen shop practices its craft with religious seriousness, and a vending machine serves hot soup. The city is enormous but never rude: everyone flows quietly, every corner is clean, even getting lost is safe. Tokyo's secret is not in its scale but in its detail — the closer you look, the more you see.

local_word.definition: The philosophy of Japanese hospitality: service considered before you ask, given without expectation of return. The taxi door that opens by itself, the cashier presenting your package with both hands, the paper bag slipped into plastic when it rains — all omotenashi. There is no tipping, because excellence is already the standard.

rules.title: Flow quietly: no phone calls on the train, no eating while walking
rules.description: Tokyo's order runs on invisible rules: no phone conversations on the metro, food eaten standing rather than strolling, and your trash travels in your bag — bins are rare. Compliance is the tourist's invisible visa: follow the rules and the city opens its doors.

rules.title: Carry both an IC card and cash
rules.description: A Suica or Pasmo card (loadable onto your phone) works everywhere from metro to vending machine; but small ramen shops and temples still want cash. In ticket-machine restaurants, buy your slip from the machine first — the table is set without money changing hands.

rules.title: Tour by neighborhood; don't try to finish the city
rules.description: Tokyo cannot be 'seen' in one pass: Asakusa's temple morning, Shibuya's neon night and Yanaka's old lanes are separate cities. Pick two or three neighborhoods a day and connect them by train — fewer districts, more depth: that is the Tokyo formula.

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: The green loop that rings the city

tip.label: The Tokyo philosophy
tip.text: Half plan, half discovery: a world hides behind every station's back streets. Get lost — in Tokyo it's safe, clean and usually the best story of the day. Board a train, get off at a stop you don't know.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Tokyo's rail network is the city's bloodstream: the Yamanote loop is the spine, the metro its capillaries — and a Suica card makes it all one tap.

items.title: Arriving from the airports
items.description: Haneda connects to the center in half an hour by monorail or the Keikyu line; from Narita, the Narita Express or Skyliner takes about an hour. Skip paper tickets and tap through with Suica — buy the card at the airport or load it onto your phone.

items.title: The Yamanote loop
items.description: The green loop train strings the city's main stops together: Shibuya, Shinjuku, Ueno, Tokyo Station. If you're lost, return to the Yamanote — the loop eventually delivers you to a familiar platform.

items.title: Metro mastery
items.description: Two metro companies and color-coded lines look confusing at first: follow the station numbers (like G-09); the signage is flawless. Rush hour from 07:30 to 09:00 is serious — never board with a suitcase then.

items.title: Walking the neighborhoods
items.description: Tokyo's neighborhoods open up on foot: exit the station, leave the main street, turn into the lanes. Addresses run by block, not street name — follow the map, and count getting lost as part of the program.

items.title: Day-trip Shinkansen
items.description: From Tokyo Station the bullet train reaches Kamakura, Nikko and even the Fuji foothills for day trips. The JR Pass no longer pays off for everyone — calculate your route; single tickets win on most short itineraries.

callout.label: Train tip
callout.text: Load Suica onto your phone and use the balance at vending machines too: hunting for a card at the gate is against Tokyo's tempo. The last train runs around midnight and is taken seriously — miss it and your options are a taxi, a capsule hotel, or an izakaya open till dawn.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Tokyo choosing a neighborhood means choosing a city: Shinjuku's neon, Asakusa's temple mornings, Ginza's polish — each a different Tokyo.

local_word.definition: 'The low city': the merchant and artisan quarters of the Edo era — today's Asakusa, Yanaka and Ueno. Narrow lanes, small workshops, neighborhood bathhouses and a spirit of community still live here. The antidote to skyscraper Tokyo is shitamachi's slow rhythm.

items.name: Shinjuku
items.description: The world's busiest station, neon streets, izakaya alleys and the mini-bars of Golden Gai: the heart of Tokyo's intensity. Connected to every line — high energy, streets open till dawn.

items.name: Shibuya
items.description: The famous crossing, fashion streets and nightlife: young Tokyo's showcase. Harajuku and Omotesando in walking distance — the tempo is high and boredom impossible.

items.name: Asakusa
items.description: The neighborhood of Senso-ji temple: temple courtyards in the morning, shutters closing early, quiet nights. Friendly prices and ryokan options — for waking up in the shitamachi spirit.

items.name: Ginza and Tokyo Station
items.description: Luxury windows, Michelin basements and the Imperial Palace walk: Tokyo's most refined bank. Next to Tokyo Station, the shinkansen gateway — comfort and location at their peak.

items.name: Ueno and Yanaka
items.description: The museum park, the Ameyoko market street and Yanaka's old-Tokyo lanes: little tourist polish, plenty of character. On the Yamanote — a calm, authentic base.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Tokyo's calendar knows two peaks: late-March sakura and November koyo — but the city runs full twelve months, and every season tells it differently.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Sakura Wave
items.subtitle: Spring · Hanami picnics, mild days
items.description: In late March and early April the sakura paints the city pink: hanami picnics fill the parks and the canals brim with petals. The peak lasts a week and the world comes for it — so do prices and crowds. May is the green, calm back door.

callout.label: Sakura note
callout.text: Book sakura-week rooms months ahead and follow the forecast maps: the peak shifts every year. If Ueno and the Meguro Canal are packed, go at 07:00 — the same pink, an empty path. And mind Golden Week (late April–early May): everything fills.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Matsuri and Humidity
items.subtitle: Summer · Festival drums, fireworks, sticky air
items.description: Summer Tokyo is humid and hot, but it pays you back: neighborhood matsuri festivals, yukata evenings and fireworks over the rivers. Air-conditioned museum-and-cafe breaks are part of the program — early morning and late evening is summer's formula.

callout.label: July tip
callout.text: If you catch the Sumida River fireworks night, claim your spot hours early or find a bridge away from the crowds. Buy yakisoba and kakigori (shaved ice) from the matsuri stalls — summer Tokyo tastes of festival streets.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Koyo Crimson
items.subtitle: Autumn · Clear skies, crimson maple gardens
items.description: October cools and November paints the city crimson and gold: maple gardens, ginkgo avenues and crystal views of Fuji. This is Tokyo's most balanced touring window — smaller crowds than sakura, and even finer light.

callout.label: November tip
callout.text: In late November check the night illuminations of the Rikugien and Koishikawa gardens: the crimson maples glow like paintings floating in the dark. The ginkgo tunnel of Meiji Jingu Gaien turns gold the same weeks.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Clear and Quiet
items.subtitle: Winter · Dry cold, crystal Fuji views, warm izakayas
items.description: Tokyo winter is dry and sunny: the sky stays clear, and Fuji shows crystal-sharp from the observation decks. The New Year temple visits (hatsumode) are among the city's truest traditions — hotels run calmer than summer and the izakayas are steamy and warm.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: Go up an observation deck early on a January morning: in winter air, Fuji rises postcard-sharp above the city. Shake off the evening cold at an oden stall or in ramen steam — winter is Tokyo's soup season.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Tokyo holds more Michelin stars than any city on earth, but its real miracle is how extraordinary the ordinary places are: even the station ramen man is a craftsman.

local_word.definition: 'I leave it to you': the art of surrendering the menu to the chef. Say omakase at a sushi bar and the chef builds you a personal course from the day's best fish — mastery in exchange for trust. Stating your budget up front is not rude; omakase can be lavish, or a surprising lunchtime bargain.

items.name: Sushi: from counter to omakase
items.description: From Toyosu market's morning sushi to the neighborhood master's counter: fresh fish is the baseline here; craft is the difference. Standing sushi bars (tachigui) are excellent and affordable — eating nigiri with your hand is legitimate, and dipping fish-side into the soy is the etiquette.
items.tag: At the counter · soy on the fish side

items.name: The ramen ritual
items.description: Buy a slip from the ticket machine, take a counter seat, wait for your bowl: from tonkotsu to shoyu, each shop masters one soup. Slurping isn't rude, it's a compliment — and a queue means you're at the right door.
items.tag: Slip from the machine · slurping welcome

items.name: Izakaya night
items.description: At the Japanese tavern the small plates keep coming: yakitori skewers, edamame, karaage fried chicken. Start with 'toriaezu nama' (a beer, to begin) — the izakaya is where Tokyo exhales after work.
items.tag: Small plates · a beer to begin

items.name: Konbini breakfast
items.description: 7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart: the Japanese convenience store is a kitchen — onigiri, the famous egg sandwich (tamago sando) and hot coffee. Cheap, fresh and astonishingly good: whoever scorns the konbini misses Tokyo's first lesson.

items.name: Depachika discovery
items.description: The basement food halls of the luxury department stores: bento boxes, mochi sweets, a hundred kinds of pickles. Discount stickers appear near closing time — a depachika bento eaten in a park is Tokyo's elegant picnic trick.

items.name: Wagashi and a matcha pause
items.description: Wagashi, the delicate sweets shaped by the season, beside a deep bowl of matcha: at a temple tea house or an old confectioner's. Sweet first, tea after — bitterness and sweetness speak in turn.
items.tag: Tea-house grace · shaped by the season

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: In Tokyo the lunch sets (teishoku) deliver mastery at half the evening price: schedule the big meal for noon. Queues signal quality and the plastic food displays decode the menu — and remember: no tipping; thanks are said with 'gochisosama deshita'.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees Shibuya Crossing; these six are Tokyo's old-laned, valley-voiced hidden face.

items.name: Yanaka Ginza
items.description: The market street of a shitamachi quarter that survived war and earthquake: cat figurines, craft shops, and the 'sunset stairs' in evening light. With its temple courtyards and cedar-shaded old cemetery — Tokyo's slowest afternoon.

items.name: Shimokitazawa
items.description: Second-hand record shops, vintage stores, tiny stages and coffee roasters: Tokyo's bohemian village. Two stops from the main lines, years away in atmosphere — Sunday afternoon is its liveliest hour.

items.name: Todoroki Valley
items.description: A stream valley shaded by bamboo and maple in the middle of Setagaya: a footpath, a red bridge and a temple tea house at the valley's end. The metropolis' sound disappears in thirty seconds — Tokyo's most surprising nature escape.

items.name: Kagurazaka
items.description: The stone lanes of an old geisha district now filled with French bistros and kappo restaurants: Tokyo's 'little Paris'. The red-lantern staircases in its side alleys are the evening walk's reward.

items.name: The Nezu Museum garden
items.description: An Asian art collection beside Omotesando, with a hidden Japanese garden behind: tea houses, mossy stones, a lotus pond. From fashion's heart to stillness in two minutes — the elegant summary of Tokyo's contrasts.

items.name: Omoide Yokocho
items.description: A narrow postwar izakaya alley at the foot of Shinjuku Station: smoke, lantern light and shoulder-to-shoulder counters. It earns its name, 'Memory Lane' — a yakitori skewer and a beer are the ticket for time travel.

callout.label: Contrast strategy
callout.text: Tour Tokyo by contrast: balance a neon morning with an old quarter, a packed crossing with a garden. From Shibuya to Todoroki, Shinjuku to Kagurazaka — two opposite Tokyos in one day is the city's true portrait.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Tokyo is among the world's most honest cities; its traps are few but wearying for the unprepared — keep these four in your pocket.

items.name: The Kabukicho touts
items.description: In the nightlife district, touts offering 'free drinks, great bar' (especially the English-speaking ones) steer you to venues with inflated bills; objecting is hard.
items.instead: Never follow a street invitation to a bar — keep the rule absolute. For a drinking night choose Golden Gai's signposted bars or izakaya chains; ask about the cover charge at the door, and the answer will be clear.

items.name: Tourist sushi windows
items.description: In some tourist zones, windows shouting 'fresh fish' sell mediocre sushi at master prices; an English-menu crowd can mislead.
items.instead: Choose the queued tachigui bars, the market-hall counters or the lunchtime set menus of sushi masters. Clear price list, full counter, a chef chatting with Japanese customers — that's the right place.

items.name: The reflexive JR Pass
items.description: The JR Pass price has risen: a traveler staying in Tokyo with one or two day trips never earns the pass back.
items.instead: Calculate your route: for long itineraries like a Kyoto–Osaka round trip the pass can still make sense, but for a Tokyo-focused trip Suica plus single tickets nearly always wins. Five minutes of math, serious savings.

items.name: Assuming cards work everywhere
items.description: Tokyo looks modern, but small restaurants, temples and some bars run cash-only; the card-only tourist stalls at the door.
items.instead: Always carry 10,000–20,000 yen in cash; the konbini ATMs (7-Eleven) take foreign cards without fuss. Coins help at ticket-machine shops too — cash is still a key in Tokyo.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Almost no one in Tokyo is trying to cheat you — the exceptions cluster in the night districts and tourist windows. Trust the queue, distrust the tout, carry cash: with these three, the city's honesty works entirely in your favor.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From temple morning to neon night

steps.title: Senso-ji morning
steps.description: Tour Asakusa's temple before the crowds: pass under the Kaminarimon lantern, make a wish in the incense smoke. Leave as the Nakamise shops open.

steps.title: Ueno and the Yanaka lanes
steps.description: A short dive into one of the park's museums, then an old-Tokyo walk along Yanaka Ginza: cats, craft shops, stone stairs.

steps.title: Ramen noon
steps.description: Slip from the ticket machine, seat at the counter: the day's reward in a steaming bowl. Slurp — it's a compliment.

steps.title: Meiji Shrine and Harajuku
steps.description: From the silence of the cedar forest to the sugary chaos of Takeshita Street: Tokyo's contrast in a single walk. Close with Omotesando's architectural windows.

steps.title: Shibuya Crossing and an observation deck
steps.description: First cross it from inside, then watch from above: as the lights come on, the human tide becomes a synchronized dance.

steps.title: Izakaya and Omoide Yokocho
steps.description: Yakitori and beer in the lantern alley, shoulder to shoulder at the counter: 'toriaezu nama!' If the night stretches, Golden Gai's mini-bars are two steps away.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Temples, valleys and counters — the full Tokyo

steps.title: Classic Tokyo
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Senso-ji, Yanaka, ramen, Meiji-Harajuku, Shibuya, an izakaya night.

steps.title: Market morning and the polished bank
steps.description: Sushi breakfast at Toyosu or the Tsukiji outer market; Ginza windows and a depachika hunt at noon; tea in the Nezu Museum garden in the afternoon; a kappo dinner in Kagurazaka's stone lanes at night.

steps.title: Valley, bohemian village and farewell
steps.description: Morning on the Todoroki Valley stream path with temple tea; records and vintage in Shimokitazawa in the afternoon; farewell sunset from a Shinjuku observation deck — wave to Fuji if it's clear, and close in ramen steam.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Japanese is a language of courtesy, and even one word of effort earns great respect; these five open every door a crack.

items.meaning: Hello — the daytime greeting; pair it with a slight bow
Thank you very much — 'arigatou' for short; you'll say it fifty times a day
Excuse me / sorry / thanks — Japanese's hardest-working magic word
Said before eating — the expression of gratitude to the meal; hands together
Cheers! — the opening move of an izakaya night; glasses touch lightly

checklist.title: Tokyo Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Kanpai! You've lived the city of order and neon the way it deserves!

items.label: Tour Senso-ji early in the morning
